source.title: An Empirical Study on Hyperparameters and their Interdependence for RL Generalization
source.authors: Xing-You Song; Yilun Du; Jacob Jackson

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the paper and appendix; some figures are flattened, so their precise values cannot be recovered.
record.tranche_reason: Reports RL generalization outcomes and gradient-based measurements under hyperparameter changes, using a different setting and measures from the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates RL agents on held-out MDPs from procedurally generated or synthetic families. It does not test fitting arbitrary labels or the listed supervised-learning model, optimizer, sharpness, and memorized-example claims. Figure-only curves are not converted into numerical rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own RL generalization results, but none measures a listed claim version. Its batch-size experiments concern PPO policies and held-out rewards, rather than image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets (V5). Gradient cosine similarity is neither magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness nor a ranking of generalization gaps against alternative measures (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that RL hyperparameters interact, sometimes reversing another parameter's relationship with generalization. They present GCS and other trajectory measurements as diagnostic intuition, with diminished GCS–performance correspondence under complex synthetic rewards.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use policy-gradient PPO and a synthetic RNN-MDP or procedurally generated RL environments, not the supervised-learning methods and datasets in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with action and transition stochasticity, discount factor γ, minibatch number, and regularization setting; GCS–test-performance correspondence is weaker with more complex synthetic rewards.

fits_no_version.finding: Action stochasticity and sticky actions increase GCS and decrease test loss in the synthetic RNN-MDP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Action stochasticity can improve held-out performance and training/test gradient alignment in synthetic RL.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher discount factors improve test performance with stochastic transitions, while lower factors perform better with deterministic transitions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transition stochasticity can reverse the relationship between discount factor and RL generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: CoinRun regularizers affect GCS, gradient norms, weight norms, convergence, and test performance differently.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL regularizers have distinct effects on optimization trajectories and held-out rewards; GCS is an imperfect diagnostic.

fits_no_version.finding: Minibatch count affects CoinRun test performance and GCS stability, with effects depending on action stochasticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size and action stochasticity interact in PPO generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Stochasticity narrows the discount-factor range yielding high CoinRun test performance but improves performance at larger discount factors in RandomMazes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The interaction between discount factor and stochasticity depends on the RL environment.

record.peer_reviewed: ICML 2019 Workshop on Understanding and Improving Generalization in Deep Learning
record.problems: The paper characterizes several results qualitatively and supplies many outcomes only as plots; precise values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the supplied text. The authors state that gradient cosine similarity can fail to correlate with test performance under more complex reward functions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional figure-only values were extracted because the flattened plots do not support reliable assignment of precise values to settings.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test-error changes when widening networks beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Large-batch penalties in image classification or language modeling under fixed epoch budgets, and recipe adaptations that remove them.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error and interactions with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; this does not deny the reported RL effects. The record's blanket PPO recipe description needs qualification: Appendix A.2.1 specifies SGD or full-batch GD for the synthetic RNN-MDP experiments. No additional result bearing on a listed version was identified.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization alongside generalization on natural labels; listed models and datasets.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation on one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on image or language benchmarks.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets for image classifiers or language models.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of train-test gaps.
Removing highly memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: RNN-MDP policy
rows.operation_detail: Varied action stochasticity and sticky actions during training.

conditions.value: random or sticky actions; probabilities shown on figure legend

rows.measure: Gradient cosine similarity and test loss
rows.value: Adding stochasticity increased GCS and decreased test loss; precise values figure only.
rows.locator: Section 3.1.1; Figure 1; Appendix A.1.2; Figure A1
rows.note: Authors explicitly describe the direction of both outcomes; no numerical values stated in text.
rows.check: The qualitative stochasticity result is supported, but measures no listed version. GRU-512 describes the fixed environment transition model; the trained policy is a 2–4-layer ReLU MLP (Appendix A.2.1).

rows.subject: RNN-MDP policy
rows.operation_detail: Varied reward discount factor γ under deterministic versus stochastic state transitions.
rows.value: Higher γ produced better generalization with transition stochasticity; lower γ produced better generalization in the deterministic setting.
rows.locator: Section 3.1.1; Figure 2; Appendix A.1.2.1; Figure A2
rows.note: The direction of the γ relationship reverses across the two transition settings.
rows.check: The reversal of the discount-factor relationship across transition settings is supported, but measures no listed version. GRU-512 describes the environment, not the trained policy. Split deterministic and stochastic conditions into separate rows.

rows.subject: CoinRun policy
rows.operation_detail: Measured gradient cosine similarity over training across regularization and training settings.

conditions.value: normal training, batch normalization, batch normalization with stochasticity 0.1, stochasticity 0.1, data augmentation

rows.measure: Gradient cosine similarity and test performance
rows.baseline: normal training (condition shown); exact values not stated
rows.value: Steadily decreasing GCS was associated with worse testing performance; higher asymptotic GCS correlated with test performance.
rows.note: The paper reports a correlation, not that GCS determines test performance.
rows.check: GCS–reward association measures no listed version. Section 3.2.1 associates decreasing GCS with worse performance, whereas Appendix A.1.5.1 associates monotonically decreasing GCS with better performance than unstable trajectories. Preserve this distinction and avoid causal wording.

rows.subject: CoinRun policy
rows.operation_detail: Added data augmentation during policy training.
rows.measure: Gradient cosine similarity, gradient norm, network norm, entropy, and convergence
rows.baseline: normal training (condition shown); exact values not stated
rows.value: Data augmentation produced constant non-zero GCS and high asymptotic gradient norm, did not significantly deviate network norm or entropy, and did not allow the policy to converge.
rows.locator: Section 3.2.1; Figure A3 cited in text
rows.note: The text states the outcome qualitatively; no numerical values are provided.
rows.check: The reported augmentation effects measure no listed version. This row combines multiple measures. The text cites Figure A3, but the relevant regularizer metrics appear in Figures 3–4; Figure A3 concerns instability.

rows.subject: CoinRun policy
rows.operation_detail: Added action stochasticity and compared gradient and network measurements.
rows.measure: GCS, test performance, policy entropy, network weight L2 norm, and gradient norm
rows.baseline: normal training (condition shown); exact values not stated
rows.value: Stochasticity improved GCS and was associated with higher eventual test performance; it did not change network weight L2 norm. Batch normalization changed weight norms, reduced GCS variance and magnitude, and reduced gradient norm.
rows.note: The authors describe the stochasticity–test-performance relation as a correlation. Outcomes for batch normalization are recorded as a separate condition in this row.
rows.check: These regularization and gradient results measure no listed version. Split stochasticity, batch normalization, and their combination, and separate held-out performance from gradient and weight measurements.

rows.subject: CoinRun policy
rows.operation_detail: Varied minibatch count while holding training stochasticity at 0.1.
rows.value: Minibatch number had a strong effect on test performance; larger batchsize produced significantly more GCS variance. At nminibatch = 64, GCS was negligible due to too much noise from low batchsize.
rows.note: The paper reports qualitative effects but does not state exact test-reward values in text.
rows.check: PPO minibatch effects on reward do not measure V5's fixed-epoch classification or language-model claim. Figure 5 uses stochasticity 0.1, while Figure 6 compares 0.0 and 0.2; separate these conditions. The qualitative test-performance statement does not establish a monotonic batch-size penalty.

rows.subject: CoinRun policy
rows.operation_detail: Varied reward discount factor γ at different forced action-stochasticity levels.
rows.value: Higher stochasticity narrowed the range of γ values associated with high test performance.
rows.note: The text does not provide numerical rewards or a complete account of which γ values performed best.
rows.check: The discount-factor interaction measures no listed version. Specify that forced action stochasticity was applied during both training and testing, rather than only during training.

rows.subject: RandomMazes policy
rows.operation_detail: Varied reward discount factor γ at two action-stochasticity levels.
rows.value: Stochasticity improved the larger γ ranges for test performance.
rows.note: Qualitative direction stated; exact values are figure-only.
rows.check: The RandomMazes discount-factor interaction measures no listed version. The appendix applies the same training/testing stochasticity protocol as the preceding CoinRun experiment.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
